body:
Earth as a planet

The Earth is a rocky planet that formed approximately 4.54 billion years ago, or 454 crore years ago. It developed as part of the formation of the Solar System rather than as an independent celestial body.

The Earth has undergone continuous physical, chemical and biological changes since its formation. Its present continents, oceans, atmosphere and living organisms developed gradually over geological time.

Origin of the universe and origin of the Earth

The Big Bang Theory explains the development of the universe from an extremely hot and dense early state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. As the universe expanded and cooled, conditions developed for the formation of atoms, stars and galaxies.

The Solar System formed much later, approximately 4.6 billion years ago, from a cloud of gas and dust within the Milky Way galaxy.

The Big Bang Theory explains the origin and early development of the universe. The nebular explanation concerns the formation of the Solar System, including the Earth. These are explanations of different events.

The nebular explanation of planetary formation

A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space. The widely accepted explanation of Solar System formation involves the gravitational collapse of such a cloud and the subsequent accumulation of material into planets.

  1. Gravitational collapse: Gas and dust were drawn together under the influence of gravity.
  2. Formation of a rotating disc: The collapsing material developed into a rotating disc. Most of the material accumulated near its centre, where the Sun formed.
  3. Formation of planetesimals: Small solid particles collided and joined together, gradually developing into larger bodies called planetesimals.
  4. Accretion: Through repeated collisions and gravitational attraction, smaller bodies accumulated into larger planetary bodies.
  5. Planetary formation: The growing bodies developed into planets, including the early Earth.

Accretion is the process through which matter accumulates to form a progressively larger body. It played a central role in the formation of planets.

Early explanations of the Earth's origin

Several historical hypotheses attempted to explain planetary formation. Their basic distinctions are useful for matching scientists with their ideas.

HypothesisAssociated contributorsBasic idea
Early nebular hypothesisImmanuel Kant and Pierre-Simon LaplacePlanets developed from rotating gaseous material.
Historical planetesimal hypothesisThomas Chamberlin and Forest MoultonA stellar encounter removed material from the Sun, which subsequently formed planetary bodies.
Revised nebular explanationsOtto Schmidt and Carl Friedrich von WeizsackerGas and dust surrounding the Sun contributed to planetary formation.

Kant presented his explanation in 1755, and Laplace developed a related hypothesis in 1796. Modern planetary science supports formation through a rotating disc and accretion, rather than the historical explanation that a passing star pulled planetary material from the Sun.

How the Moon formed

The leading scientific explanation for the formation of the Moon is the Giant Impact Hypothesis. According to this explanation, a large planetary body collided with the young Earth. Material released into orbit subsequently accumulated to form the Moon. The exact details of this event remain under scientific investigation.

Prelims focus

  • Estimated age of the Earth: approximately 4.54 billion years.
  • Estimated age of the universe: approximately 13.8 billion years.
  • Kant and Laplace are associated with early nebular explanations.
  • Planetesimals are small bodies involved in planetary formation.
  • Accretion involves the accumulation of matter into larger bodies.
  • Giant Impact Hypothesis: formation of the Moon.

Trap: The Big Bang did not directly form the Earth or the other planets.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 2, The Origin and Evolution of the Earth, sections on early theories and formation of planets; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 8–11; US Geological Survey, Geologic Time: Age of the Earth; NASA Science, Solar System: Facts, Formation section; NASA Science, Universe Glossary, Big Bang entry; NASA Science, Moon Formation. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Origin of the Earth and the Solar System

body:
From a hot young planet to a layered Earth

The early Earth experienced intense heating during its formation. Collisions between growing planetary bodies, gravitational compression and the decay of radioactive elements contributed to this heat.

As substantial portions of the young Earth melted, its constituent materials began to separate according to their densities. Denser metallic materials, especially iron, moved towards the centre, while relatively lighter rocky materials remained above them.

This process is called differentiation. It produced the broad internal divisions of the Earth: the crust, mantle and core.

LayerGeneral compositionPosition
CrustRelatively light silicate rocksOutermost layer
MantleDenser silicate rocks rich in magnesium and ironBetween crust and core
CoreMainly iron and nickelCentral region

Accretion explains how the Earth accumulated material and grew. Differentiation explains how that material became separated into internal layers.

Development of the atmosphere

The present atmosphere did not exist in its current form when the Earth originated. Its development involved several broad stages.

Loss of the primitive atmosphere

Much of the light hydrogen and helium associated with the early Earth was lost to space. The solar wind and other atmospheric escape processes contributed to this loss.

Release of gases from the interior

As the Earth evolved, gases escaped from its interior through volcanic and related geological activity. This process is called degassing or outgassing.

Water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and other gases contributed to the development of a secondary atmosphere. Free molecular oxygen was initially present in very small quantities compared with its abundance today.

Formation of the oceans

As the Earth's surface and atmosphere cooled sufficiently, water vapour could condense into liquid water. Precipitation and the accumulation of liquid water in low-lying depressions contributed to the formation of the oceans.

Water was also incorporated into the Earth during planetary formation. The precise contributions of different sources to the Earth's original water remain under investigation.

The development of liquid water created conditions suitable for the subsequent emergence and evolution of life.

Biological modification of the atmosphere

The earliest forms of life were microscopic organisms. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis, particularly by ancient microorganisms, gradually released oxygen into the environment.

Much of the early oxygen reacted with substances in the oceans and rocks. Over geological time, oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, allowing the evolution of more complex oxygen-dependent organisms.

The major natural spheres of the Earth

  • Lithosphere: The rigid outer portion of the Earth, consisting of the crust and the uppermost rigid mantle.
  • Atmosphere: The gaseous envelope surrounding the Earth.
  • Hydrosphere: Water in the oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and other reservoirs.
  • Biosphere: The living world and the portions of the Earth in which life exists.

These spheres interact continuously. For example, rain from the atmosphere weathers rocks of the lithosphere, while rivers transport dissolved minerals and sediments into the oceans. Living organisms influence atmospheric composition and contribute to soil development.

Prelims focus

  • Differentiation separated denser metallic materials from lighter rocky materials.
  • The core is predominantly composed of iron and nickel.
  • Degassing released gases from the Earth's interior.
  • Cooling and condensation contributed to ocean formation.
  • Oxygen-producing photosynthesis increased atmospheric oxygen over geological time.

Trap: The Earth's primitive atmosphere was not rich in free oxygen like the present atmosphere.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 2, Evolution of the Earth and Evolution of Atmosphere and Hydrosphere; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 14–16; NASA Science, Facts About Earth, Formation and Structure sections. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of geological time

The Earth has existed for approximately 4.54 billion years. During this immense interval, continents have changed positions, mountains have risen and eroded, oceans have opened and closed, and numerous forms of life have appeared and become extinct.

The geological time scale divides the history of the Earth into recognised intervals. These divisions provide a common framework for describing the ages of rocks, fossils, natural resources and major geological events.

Hierarchy of geological time

Geological time is divided into units of different sizes. The principal units, from the largest to the smallest, are:

  1. Eon
  2. Era
  3. Period
  4. Epoch
  5. Age

For example, the Cenozoic is an era within the Phanerozoic Eon. The Quaternary is a period within the Cenozoic Era, and the Holocene is an epoch within the Quaternary Period.

The major divisions of Earth's history

Precambrian

The Precambrian is the collective name for the immense interval preceding the Phanerozoic Eon. It includes the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic eons.

It accounts for approximately 88% of Earth's history. During this interval, the Earth formed, its early crust and oceans developed, microscopic life appeared, and atmospheric oxygen gradually increased. Many ancient continental rocks and important mineral-bearing rock formations originated during this time.

Much of the ancient crystalline foundation of Peninsular India belongs to the Precambrian.

Paleozoic Era

The Paleozoic, also written Palaeozoic, means ancient life. It followed the Precambrian and began approximately 539 million years ago.

Marine organisms diversified, and plants and animals gradually established themselves on land. Extensive vegetation accumulated in ancient environments and contributed to the formation of important coal deposits.

The Paleozoic includes the Carboniferous and Permian periods, in that order. These are particularly useful for understanding coal-bearing rocks and the geological history of Gondwana.

Mesozoic Era

The Mesozoic extends from approximately 252 million to 66 million years ago. It is commonly called the Age of Reptiles because dinosaurs and other reptiles were prominent during this interval.

Its 3 periods, from oldest to youngest, are the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous. The fragmentation of Pangaea and the separation of several continental landmasses occurred during this era.

The first mammals also appeared during the Mesozoic. The era ended with a major mass extinction in which non-avian dinosaurs disappeared.

Cenozoic Era

The Cenozoic, commonly called the Age of Mammals, began approximately 66 million years ago and continues to the present. Mammals and birds diversified considerably during this era.

Its main periods are the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary, in that order. The collision between India and Eurasia, the major uplift of the Himalayas and the development of extensive younger sedimentary plains are important Indian geographical events associated with the Cenozoic.

Tertiary and Quaternary terminology

Older geography and geology textbooks frequently use the term Tertiary. It broadly corresponds to the combined Paleogene and Neogene periods of the Cenozoic. Tertiary is no longer used as a formal period in the modern international geological time scale, but remains common in descriptions of Indian coal, petroleum and sedimentary formations.

The Quaternary Period is younger than the traditional Tertiary interval. It began approximately 2.58 million years ago and includes the Pleistocene and Holocene epochs.

  • Pleistocene: Characterised by repeated glacial and interglacial intervals.
  • Holocene: The epoch beginning after the last major glacial interval, approximately 11,700 years ago.

Prelims focus

  • Eon is larger than era; era is larger than period.
  • Precambrian represents approximately 88% of Earth's history.
  • The Paleozoic precedes the Mesozoic, which precedes the Cenozoic.
  • Mesozoic sequence: Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous.
  • Cenozoic sequence: Paleogene, Neogene, Quaternary.
  • The Quaternary includes the Pleistocene and Holocene.

Trap: Mammals first appeared during the Mesozoic, although their major diversification is associated with the Cenozoic.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 2, Origin of Life and Geological Time Scale in the earlier textbook edition; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; International Commission on Stratigraphy, International Chronostratigraphic Chart, 2026, major time divisions, numerical boundaries rounded for orientation; US National Park Service, Geologic Time Scale and Fossils Through Geologic Time. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
